title: ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY
body:
Where the analysis half of [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and the theory half of
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] get carried further. Second year asks "what is this
structure and what does it cost"; this course asks the harder questions on top of that:
how do you *design* an algorithm rather than recall one, how do you prove a bound instead
of counting loops, and what do you do when the answer is that no fast algorithm exists.

That framing is not invented here. Twelve notes across five courses already point at this
file and say what it owns, and the sections below are built from those promises rather than
from a syllabus. **This parent is a consolidation hub**: it has no child notes of its own,
so every link goes out to the course or the book that already covers the topic. Where a
topic is promised but has no note anywhere in the vault, it is named in prose without a
link, so nothing here pretends to material that does not exist.

## Topics

### Analysis: what an algorithm costs

[[Time Complexity]] · [[Asymptotic Analysis]]

[[Time Complexity]] owns the ladder from $O(1)$ to $O(n!)$ and how to read it off a loop
nest; [[Asymptotic Analysis]] owns the machinery underneath, the three bounds and the
formal $c$ and $n_0$ definition. Both were written expecting this course to pick up
**recurrence relations and the master theorem**, the tool for costing a recursive algorithm
from its own structure rather than by counting. Neither has a note in the vault. The
technique that stands in for them is [[Proof By Induction]] in [[DISCRETE MATH]], which is
how you verify a guessed bound once you have one.

The other loose end from second year is **amortised** analysis, which [[Time Complexity]]
introduces on [[Dynamic Arrays]] (append is $O(n)$ on the resize and $O(1)$ the rest of the
time, so the cost per operation over a long run is $O(1)$). It is a different question from
the average case and the distinction is worth keeping.

### Design strategies

The four ways of attacking a problem, each with the notes that already demonstrate it:

| Strategy | The idea | Worked in |
|---|---|---|
| Divide and conquer | split, solve the halves, combine | [[Merge Sort]], [[Quick Sort]], [[Modified Binary Search]], [[Fast Fourier Transform]] |
| Greedy | take the locally best choice and never reconsider | [[Minimum Spanning Tree]] (Kruskal and Prim) |
| [[Dynamic Programming]] | solve each overlapping subproblem once and reuse it | [[Dynamic Programming]] |
| [[Backtracking]] | search every choice, prune the dead ends early | [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], [[Backtracking]] |

The interesting fact about the greedy row is that greedy is usually *wrong*, and
[[Minimum Spanning Tree]] says so out loud: both Kruskal and Prim being correct is unusual
enough to need a proof. Dynamic programming and backtracking are the same search seen from
two directions, which is why both start from [[Recursion]]: memoise a recursion and you have
dynamic programming, prune it and you have backtracking.

The divide-and-conquer row gained [[Fast Fourier Transform]] when MATH 4199 was written, and it
may be the strongest entry in the table. It runs the same recurrence as [[Merge Sort]],
$T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N)$, and takes the discrete Fourier transform from $O(N^2)$ to
$O(N \log N)$. At $N = 10^6$ that is five orders of magnitude, which is the clearest case in
the degree of an *algorithm* rather than hardware being what made an application possible.
By the [[Convolution Theorem]] it also drops convolution itself from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N\log N)$,
and with it large-filter image work and big-integer multiplication.

### Sorting

[[Sequential Sorting]] · [[Bubble Sort]] · [[Insertion Sort]] · [[Merge Sort]] ·
[[Quick Sort]] · heapsort inside [[Heap]]

[[Sequential Sorting]] is the map over the five and carries the one argument none of them
hold individually: the decision-tree proof that $\Omega(n \log n)$ is a wall for any
comparison sort, because a binary tree that must reach $n!$ distinct orderings has height at
least $\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$. The $n!$ comes from [[Permutation]].

The escape from that wall is to stop comparing. Counting sort, radix sort, and bucket sort
read the key's structure instead (its digits, or its value used directly as an index) and
run in $O(n)$ or $O(nk)$ on bounded integers. No note in the vault covers them; they belong
here and are the clearest thing this course would add to the sorting material.

### Searching

[[Search Trees]] · [[Modified Binary Search]] · [[Binary Search Tree]] · [[Balanced Tree]] ·
[[Hashing]] · [[Hash Map]] · [[Heap]] · [[Top K Elements]]

[[Search Trees]] is the which-structure-for-which-question index, and it makes the same
decision-tree argument as the sorting bound applied to a single query: $\log n$ is the height
of a binary tree with $n$ outcomes, so no comparison-based search beats it. [[Hashing]] and
radix structures (tries, which have no note anywhere) get around it by looking at the key's
bits rather than comparing whole keys. [[Top K Elements]] is the practical form of the
[[Heap]] argument: you never need to sort $n$ items to get the best $k$.

### Graph algorithms

[[Graph]] · [[Weighted Graph]] · [[Directed Graph]] · [[Vertices]] · [[Adjacency Matrix]] ·
[[Adjacency List]] · [[Breadth First Search]] · [[Depth First Search]] ·
[[Matrix Traversal]] · [[Minimum Spanning Tree]]

Second year covers *representation* and stops: [[Graph]] and [[Weighted Graph]] both say
explicitly that traversal belongs here. The traversal notes now exist in the
[[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]] set, and the split between them is the whole of it:

| | [[Breadth First Search]] | [[Depth First Search]] |
|---|---|---|
| Frontier lives in | a [[Queue]] | a [[Stack]], usually the call stack via [[Recursion]] |
| Visits | level by level | one path to its end, then backtrack |
| Gives you | fewest *edges* on an unweighted graph | reachability, cycles, connected components |

Neither gives shortest paths on a [[Weighted Graph]]. [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] does, by
swapping the queue for a [[Heap]] keyed on distance so far, and it is almost exactly Prim's
inner loop with a different quantity in the priority queue. [[Union Find]] (disjoint sets) is
the structure that makes Kruskal's "are these two already connected?" test near-constant and
the reason the edge sort dominates its running time. [[Topological Sort]] orders a DAG so
every edge points forward, which is the prerequisite problem and the setup for DP on a DAG.

All three live in `Leetcode/` as implementation notes. This course owns the *why*: the proof
that Dijkstra's greedy choice is safe under non-negative weights, why union-find's inverse
Ackermann bound is effectively constant, and what a topological order buys you.

The choice of representation is a cost decision, not a style one: $O(V^2)$ space for an
[[Adjacency Matrix]] against $O(V + E)$ for an [[Adjacency List]], which is why dense and
sparse graphs get different answers.

### Intractability

[[NP-Complete]] · [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] · [[Undecidability]] · [[Turing Machine]]

[[NP-Complete]] absorbs P vs NP and owns the definitions; [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is the
worked hard problem, with its Eulerian near-miss as the illustration that difficulty is not
predictable from how a problem is phrased. The line this course has to keep straight, and
which [[NP-Complete]] states in one sentence: **NP-complete is not undecidable**. The
algorithm exists and is merely too slow; [[Undecidability]] is about problems where no
algorithm exists at all, and that boundary belongs to [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

Counting is what makes the exponential real. [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] in
[[DISCRETE MATH]] are how you size a search space before deciding whether searching it is
hopeless: $n!$ orderings for [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], $2^n$ subsets for anything that picks a
subset.

### Pattern practice

[[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]] is the applied index over all of the above: identify the
input shape, then pick the technique. [[Prefix Sum]] · [[Two Pointers]] ·
[[Sliding Window]] · [[Monotonic Stack]] · [[Modified Binary Search]] ·
[[Overlapping Intervals]] · [[Fast and Slow Pointers]] ·
[[Linked List In-place Reversal]] · [[Binary Tree Traversal]] · [[Breadth First Search]] ·
[[Depth First Search]] · [[Matrix Traversal]] · [[Backtracking]] ·
[[Dynamic Programming]] · [[Top K Elements]]

These are interview-shaped rather than course-shaped, and that is the point: they are the
same algorithms with the analysis removed and the recognition drilled instead.

## Core Facts to Know

- Complexity is a property of the algorithm; running time is a property of the machine.
- $O$ is an upper bound, $\Omega$ a lower bound, $\Theta$ both at once.
- People write $O$ and usually mean $\Theta$.
- Worst case is the guarantee and is what "the complexity of X" means by default.
- Amortised is not the same as average: it is the cost per operation over a long run.
- Divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, and backtracking are the four design strategies.
- Greedy algorithms are usually wrong; [[Minimum Spanning Tree]] is the notable exception.
- Dynamic programming = recursion plus memoisation, so each subproblem is solved once.
- Backtracking = recursion plus pruning, so dead branches are abandoned early.
- No comparison sort beats $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case.
- The proof is a decision tree: $n!$ leaves, so height at least $\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$.
- Non-comparison sorts (counting, radix, bucket) beat that bound by reading the key, not comparing it.
- The same decision-tree argument bounds comparison-based *search* at $\Omega(\log n)$.
- [[Hashing]] escapes that bound the same way radix sorting does, by looking at the key itself.
- [[Breadth First Search]] uses a [[Queue]]; [[Depth First Search]] uses a [[Stack]].
- BFS gives the fewest edges on an *unweighted* graph, not the shortest weighted path.
- Dijkstra is BFS with a [[Heap]] keyed on distance, and its inner loop is Prim's.
- A spanning tree of $V$ vertices always has exactly $V - 1$ edges.
- Kruskal is $O(E \log E)$ and better on sparse graphs; Prim is $O(E \log V)$ and better on dense ones.
- [[Adjacency Matrix]] costs $O(V^2)$ space; [[Adjacency List]] costs $O(V + E)$.
- P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time.
- NP is the class of problems whose *proposed answers* are checkable in polynomial time.
- NP-complete = in NP, and everything in NP reduces to it.
- Finding a [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is NP-complete; checking a proposed one is $O(V)$.
- An Eulerian circuit (every *edge* once) has a one-line test: every vertex has even degree.
- NP-complete is not undecidable. The algorithm exists, it is just too slow.
- Reduction is the tool for both: it proves hardness here and unsolvability in [[Undecidability]].
- Counting ([[Permutation]], [[Combination]]) is how you size a search space before searching it.

## Related courses

- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], the direct prerequisite. It owns every structure this course
  runs algorithms on: [[Tree]], [[Graph]], [[Heap]], [[Hash Map]], [[Balanced Tree]], and
  the sort notes. [[Time Complexity]] and [[Asymptotic Analysis]] start there.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]], the other half of the theory. [[NP-Complete]],
  [[Turing Machine]], [[Undecidability]], and reduction as a proof technique.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]]: [[Proof By Induction]] for bounds on recursive algorithms, [[Sets]] for
  the definition of a [[Graph]], [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] for search-space size.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: [[Algorithm]], [[Recursion]], [[Data Structure]],
  [[Stack]], [[Queue]], [[Linked List]], where all of this is first implemented.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Sequential Sorting]], [[Search Trees]],
  [[Minimum Spanning Tree]], the self-study treatments of the same material.
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: scheduling is algorithm design under a different name, and
  [[Amdahl's Law]] is the complexity argument for parallelism.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]]: gradient descent is an optimisation algorithm, analysed the same way.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) owns [[Fast Fourier Transform]], the
  divide-and-conquer algorithm above, and [[Convolution Theorem]], which is why it is worth
  running. That course also supplies the [[Mandelbrot Set]]'s escape-time algorithm as a
  worked example of a *semi*-decision procedure.
- [[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]]: the applied index over this whole course.
